title: Running through August 15th at Atlantic Theatre Company #theatre #art...
transcript: A pair of altar boys played by actual teenagers, where their close and somewhat codependent friendship gets strained by a crisis of faith and a crisis sexuality. Meanwhile, a mysterious man take shelter in the church, raising even more questions about forgiveness, honesty and Christian charity. The Saviors is a new play from the same writer director team as the hit Well, I'll Let You Go, and I wasn't quite as moved by this one, but it achieved a similar effect of quietly sneaking under my skin and leaving a surprising impact. What Bubba Weiler maybe does most skillfully here is making these different crises and doubts that the characters are going through feel intertwined, even when they don't appear to be on the surface. There's a sense that these questions are all bumping up against each other in the characters’ heads as they try to figure out who they are and what's important to them. The other thing I'd say is that it's the sort of way that you can take a lot of different things away from depending on the experiences you walk into the room with, from the religious themes, the queer themes and even just the exploration of young masculinity. For me, a lot of the tension came from the fact that these 14 year olds are very intelligent and thoughtful, but they're still too young to fully communicate and process what they're going through. So there's this quiet delicacy to the play that's charged underneath with adolescent frustration. And that's a trope or device that I've always found really haunting and tragic: To watch all these events unfold and know that these characters won't be able to grasp it and unpack it for years to come. For those who know the movie Close it reminded me a lot of that. Except it's the social dynamics of a church rather than, like, a schoolyard.
classificationReason: Creator offers a first-hand review of The Saviors at Atlantic Theatre Company, comparing it to a prior work by the same writer-director and giving clear critical opinion on craft and themes.
